column3: The Hebrew leaves the recipient of the oil unnamed; BSB supplies Saul in “Saul’s head.”
The Hebrew explicitly refers to abandoning “the matters of the donkeys”; BSB renders this as stopping worrying about them.
Close to the Hebrew.
The Hebrew says they will ask about his “peace” or welfare; BSB says they will “greet” him. It uses singular “their hand,” rendered plural “their hands” in BSB.
The Hebrew names the harp, tambourine, flute, and lyre in the singular; BSB makes all four plural. It also uses a plural expression for the Philistine stations, where BSB has “an outpost.”
Close to the Hebrew.
The Hebrew commands doing what “your hand finds”; BSB replaces this bodily image with “as the occasion demands.”
The Hebrew explicitly describes going down to Gilgal and Samuel coming down to him; BSB leaves both downward directions implicit.
The Hebrew leaves Saul unnamed and describes his turning with “his shoulder.” God changes for him “another heart”; BSB supplies Saul’s name and says God “changed Saul’s heart.”
The Hebrew leaves the arriving travelers unnamed; BSB identifies them as Saul and his servant.
The Hebrew describes prior knowledge with “yesterday, the day before yesterday”; BSB uses “formerly.”
Close to the Hebrew.
The Hebrew leaves Saul unnamed and says he came to the high place; BSB names Saul and supplies the upward direction in “went up.”
The Hebrew leaves the respondent unnamed; BSB identifies him as Saul.
The Hebrew includes a request particle in “tell me, please”; BSB leaves the politeness particle implicit.
The Hebrew leaves the subject of not telling unnamed and uses “him” as the recipient; BSB explicitly names Saul and his uncle in that clause.
Close to the Hebrew.
The Hebrew uses singular “hand” twice and names Egypt collectively; BSB uses plural “hands” and “the Egyptians.”
The Hebrew calls the family groups “your thousands”; BSB renders this as “clans.”
Close to the Hebrew.
The Hebrew says passively that he “was not found”; BSB changes this to active “they could not find him.”
Close to the Hebrew.
The Hebrew leaves the fetched man unnamed and describes his height from his shoulder upward. BSB supplies Saul and renders the height as “a head taller.”

The Hebrew calls the dissenters “sons of worthlessness” and says he was “like one keeping silent.” BSB uses “worthless men” and says Saul “remained silent about it.” The Hebrew has singular “a gift,” rendered plural “gifts” in BSB.
